fleetMemory.LESSON: A TEST THAT HAND-BUILDS THE INPUT CANNOT SEE THE DEPLOYED INPUT. P-334's defect was invisible to a full green suite because every test gave the resolver a complete environment -- the tests asserted behaviour on inputs the deployed job never has, and the job refused on its first execution instead. The fix that makes this class of defect visible is not more assertions but reading the INPUT from the artifact that defines it: the test parses the job's SECRETS list out of cloudbuild.publish.yaml and hands the watch exactly that. Worth generalising: for any deployed job, the environment/config under test should be READ from the deploy template, never assembled by the test.

A CONTROL THAT CANNOT RESOLVE ITS OWN BASE MUST REFUSE, NOT SKIP. The pin-comment check was skipped (or crashed) on exactly the force-push it exists to see, because the workflow passed an unreachable sha and had an `if:` that skipped the null case. Two separate mechanisms, both silently turning 'cannot see' into 'no finding'. The rule worth keeping: a check that cannot see its input fails (exit 2 with a reason); a check that needs a fallback derives it from the ONE base that shows the branch's own changes (the merge-base with the declared ref), never from a branch tip.

A STORE-LESS REFUSAL LEAVES NO ROW, SO THE EXIT STATUS IS THE ONLY CHANNEL -- and that is an argument for making the code a property of the REFUSAL, not of the caller. P-322 requires parcel-ag-valuation to refuse before opening a store, so no runs row and no run event exists; a parent could only have scraped stderr (rejected: it makes the decision depend on log text, and a scrape that matched nothing looks exactly like a crash). Putting the mapping in ONE module (src/lib/scope-refusal-exits.mjs) and making src/cli.mjs exit with it means the same refusal carries the same status in the county runner, in the Cloud Run job, and under an operator's hand invocation.

A TEST'S FAKE MUST KEY THE IDENTIFIERS THE CODE ACTUALLY USES. P-330's fake Cloud Run keyed executions by the full resource name while the runner waits on the SHORT execution name, and every 'the run must stop' case looked like a pass until that was fixed. A fake that answers a different question than the code asks is green for the wrong reason -- the same failure shape as the test that hand-builds the environment.

WHEN A TEST FAILS, DECIDE WHETHER THE TEST OR THE CODE IS WRONG, AND SAY WHICH. P-330's first red run was BOTH: two assertions were wrong (a job count and the case-4 fixture pointed at a job that declares nothing) and one was a real defect (the runner set its lastExecution/lastJob bookkeeping on the failure path, so a stopped step was recorded as succeeded/refused). Recording that distinction in the close is what stops a later reader from assuming the tests were simply bent to fit.
